extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges studying patent subject-matter principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what kinds of inventions or discoveries are proper subjects of letters-patent, including distinctions among art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, and doctrines such as double use and improvements. Explains tests for novelty, application of principles, combinations, and improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of patentable cases
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a large class of cases where improvements or inventions in the mode of producing a particular known effect will be patentable; and another large class where the discovery and application of new means of producing an effect before unknown will be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One class embraces new application of known agents leading to a change in the series of processes by which a result or manufacture is produced (i.e., new method of producing a known effect). The other embraces discovery and application of new agents or things by which a new effect or result is produced. Examples: application of electricity for telegraphy (known agent applied to produce a wholly new effect) and photography (use of light to produce new kinds of pictures).

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes an application of a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether an alleged invention or discovery will support a patent, ask (1) how must the principle be made use of, and (2) what must be the result produced? Distinguish between a principle and the embodiment of a principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The embodiment of a principle so that it may act and produce an effect may be the subject of a patent; the principle itself (truth of science or law of matter) is distinct from the practice founded on it. In analyzing such inventions determine whether the agents employed are newly-discovered or well known, whether they are applied in a new method, and whether as applied they produce a new or an old result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-use doctrine (known principle applied to a new occasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new application of a known principle may be only a 'double use' which cannot be the subject of a patent if the principle has been discovered and applied before and the new application leads to no new manufacture or new result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To escape the double-use objection the new occasion or purpose must not be merely analogous to former occasions. Applying an old contrivance to a new object that is merely analogous is not patentable. Examples and illustrations: using a known wheel on railways (not patentable if merely analogous), applying an old hair-curling process to palm-leaf (not patentable), a medicine known for one disease later found to cure another (not patentable merely as a new use). The surgeon/scissors analogy shows courts will scrutinize whether the use is genuinely novel rather than analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of effect requirement when agents are known
rubrics_metrics.description: When the principle is well known or the application consists in the use of a known thing to produce a particular effect, the question is whether the effect itself is entirely new or merely the occasion is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the occasion is new (analogous use), the use is not patentable. If the effect produced by the known agent is new (no known analogous uses), then the process may constitute a patentable art. Example: use of gas to singe lace produced a new effect and was patentable, whereas scissors cutting different substances produced analogous effects and were not new for that purpose. Great discrimination is required to assess analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory classification: 'Art' (new and useful art)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Art' includes any new and useful art or any new and useful improvement of an art; it embraces cases where application of a principle is the most important part of the invention and where machinery is incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to instances where the invention is primarily a new process or method of producing an effect (even if the result or manufactured article is old). Example: printing bank-notes with copperplate and letter-press on both sides as a new method to secure against counterfeiting was held to be an 'art'. If machinery or the article produced is principally new, the subject will fall under machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory classification: 'Machine'
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine as subject of a patent must be a particular construction of mechanism containing the improved method of producing an old effect or a method of producing a new effect; it is a function embodied in particular mechanism whose mode of operation and structure are pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'machine' includes new combinations of machines and new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. A machine patent may cover a new machine even if constituent machines are old, so long as the combination or organization is new. Example: telescope combining convex and concave glasses. What constitutes a claim for a combination only versus parts of a machine is a question of construction on the patent and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents: scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention consists of a new combination of existing machinery, the thing patented is the combination; the separate machines are not the patented thing unless the patent also claims them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent claims only the combination, using any of the machines separately (without the whole combination) is not infringement. Conversely, where a patent covers several distinct and independent improvements in the same machine taken in the aggregate, the patent will protect each improvement. Whether the patent is for the combination only or includes specified improvements affects remedies and infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement of a machine: what qualifies as patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'improvement' of a machine (or an improved machine) is where an addition or alteration is made to a specific existing machine to produce the same effects better, or to produce new effects or materially superior effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent for an improvement is limited to the improvement or new combination. The key inquiry is whether the improvement is real and material or only a change of form; courts must ascertain boundaries between what was known and what is new in the mode of operation. Whether an improvement is trifling or important is typically a jury question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for whether an improvement is substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the improved machine operates upon the same principle as the former machine — i.e., whether it produces the same effect by the same mechanical means or whether a new element, combination, or feature has been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect is the same, ask whether the modus operandi and combination of powers are substantially the same. If the effect is different, the character and importance of that effect are the test of sufficiency. A machine may externally resemble another but still operate on a different principle. Examples: raising water by lever vs screw/pulley/wedge are different principles despite possible external similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for whole machine vs specific improvements: scope and potential invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee claims the whole of a machine as his invention while only parts or certain improvements are actually his invention, the patent may be void for exceeding the invention; conversely, where the whole machine is substantially new, piracy of a part may still be actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patent is for several distinct improvements which are clearly specified, piracy of any one improvement may violate the patentee's right. Where a patent is for a new combination only, unless that combination is substantially violated, the patentee has no remedy for use of separate parts. Courts examine whether the patent's terms exceed the patentee's true invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When application of known agents is patentable due to new contrivances or arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where principal agents are well known, new contrivances, combinations, or arrangements used with them may constitute a new principle and render the application patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is novelty in the preparation or arrangement of the agent, the application or practice will be new. Examples cited include using anthracite and hot-air blast in iron manufacture (novel practice), omission or different combination of ingredients in cloth manufacture, and application of steam to propel boats; such changes in combination or arrangement may sustain patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification choice determined by principal characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper statutory class (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) for a patent claim depends on the invention's principal characteristics and objects: whether application of a principle, particular machinery, or a new article/result is the core of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If application of a principle is central and machinery incidental, classify as 'art'. If machinery/structure is chief, classify as 'machine'. If the article/result produced is new, classify as 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' as appropriate. The principal characteristic controls classification and thus framing of claims.
